subject: We’re required by law to report our fundraising data after Dec 31st.

body:
Come January, I have not a single doubt that my opponent and Trump’s MAGA cronies will be refreshing the FEC site to see if our people-powered movement has the momentum to win
#
Peter, I’ll cut straight to the chase.
**On December 31st, our campaign faces a critical fundraising deadline. Here’s why this matters:**
After our deadline, we will be required, by law, to report our fundraising data to the Federal Election Commission, or the FEC. Soon after, those numbers will be posted publicly for everyone to see.
Yes, that includes Raja Krishnamoorthi, my MAGA-funded Democratic opponent. People like Donald Trump and ICE commander Gregory Bovino, who want nothing more than to keep me away from Washington. And of course, the public and our supporters, including you. It’s a big deal.
But that’s not the only reason why this deadline matters. This is **our FINAL quarterly FEC fundraising deadline before the primary election, and our final chance to show all the naysayers that our grassroots movement has what it takes to beat a Corporate PAC and MAGA-backed opponent.**
Come January, I have not a single doubt that my opponent and Trump’s MAGA cronies will be refreshing the FEC site to see if our people-powered movement has the momentum to win. They want to see soft numbers. They want proof that grassroots organizing isn’t enough to defeat special interests.
I refuse to let that be true.
But to be transparent: at our current pace, we’re projected to fall short of where we need to be before we file. And that gap can only be closed if the people who believe in this movement step up with whatever they can.
If you’re wondering whether $5 or $10 makes a difference, hear me clearly: it does. Our campaign is powered by teachers, students, nurses, organizers, retirees — and every dollar adds up when we’re all pitching in.
So as we head into the home stretch of this campaign, I’m asking from the heart:
**[Will you split a $15 contribution today between my campaign and State Democrats Committee and help us file a report that reflects the strength and determination of our movement on December 31st?](https://act.lucaskunce.com/go/99044?refcode=em20251230-9890&firstname=Peter&lastname=Willis&email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=18326&city=Cresco&state=PA&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=1&akid=9890%2E614464%2E6S2SOO)**
What we show on December 31st will define the narrative heading into the heart of this primary election. So let’s show up strong — together.
With gratitude,
Juliana Stratton

body:
Jim Jordan, Steve Scalise, Tom Emmer, Derrick Van Orden, and Eli Crane all reached out.
_Jim Jordan reached out ..._ _Steve Scalise reached out ..._ _Tom Emmer reached out ..._ _Anna Paulina Luna reached out ..._ _Richard Hudson reached out ..._ _Derrick Van Orden reached out ..._ _Eli Crane reached out ..._

| | Dorian Gray glanced at the picture, and suddenly an uncontrollable feeling of hatred for Basil Hallward came over him, as though it had been suggested to him by the image on the canvas, whispered into his ear by those grinning lips. The mad passions of a hunted animal stirred within him, and he loathed the man who was seated at the table, more than in his whole life he had ever loathed anything. He glanced wildly around. Something glimmered on the top of the painted chest that faced him. His eye fell on it. He knew what it was. It was a knife that he had brought up, some days before, to cut a piece of cord, and had forgotten to take away with him. He moved slowly towards it, passing Hallward as he did so. As soon as he got behind him, he seized it and turned round. Hallward stirred in his chair as if he was going to rise. He rushed at him and dug the knife into the great vein that is behind the ear, crushing the man’s head down on the table and stabbing again and again. There was a stifled groan and the horrible sound of some one choking with blood. Three times the outstretched arms shot up convulsively, waving grotesque, stiff-fingered hands in the air. He stabbed him twice more, but the man did not move. Something began to trickle on the floor. He waited for a moment, still pressing the head down. Then he threw the knife on the table, and listened. He could hear nothing, but the drip, drip on the threadbare carpet. He opened the door and went out on the landing. The house was absolutely quiet. No one was about. For a few seconds he stood bending over the balustrade and peering down into the black seething well of darkness. Then he took out the key and returned to the room, locking himself in as he did so. The thing was still seated in the chair, straining over the table with bowed head, and humped back, and long fantastic arms. Had it not been for the red jagged tear in the neck and the clotted black pool that was slowly widening on the table, one would have said that the man was simply asleep. How quickly it had all been done! He felt strangely calm, and walking over to the window, opened it and stepped out on the balcony. The wind had blown the fog away, and the sky was like a monstrous peacock’s tail, starred with myriads of golden eyes. He looked down and saw the policeman going his rounds and flashing the long beam of his lantern on the doors of the silent houses. The crimson spot of a prowling hansom gleamed at the corner and then vanished. A woman in a fluttering shawl was creeping slowly by the railings, staggering as she went. Now and then she stopped and peered back. Once, she began to sing in a hoarse voice. The policeman strolled over and said something to her. She stumbled away, laughing. A bitter blast swept across the square. The gas-lamps flickered and became blue, and the leafless trees shook their black iron branches to and fro. He shivered and went back, closing the window behind him.

Ivan Dmytrovych Sirko was born in the early seventeenth century, approximately between 1605 and 1610. This is evidenced primarily by the results of research on Sirko's remains, according to which the Cossack ataman was 70-75 years old at the time of his death in 1680. The first researcher of Sirko's biography, the famous Ukrainian historian Dmytro Yavornytskyi, suggested that the future ataman was born in Sloboda Ukraine in the settlement of Merefa (now the city of Merefa, Kharkiv region). However, this is not true. Merefa was founded only in 1658, i.e. when Sirko was in his late teens. However, Sirko and his family lived in Merefa for a long time in his house, and after his death, his wife and some family members lived there. The fact that Merefa in Slobozhanshchyna is associated with the name of the Cossack Ataman is evidenced by another name for the town recorded in some Ukrainian chronicles, Sirkivka. Where, then, should we look for Sirko's homeland? In our opinion, the sources give grounds to localize it in Eastern Podillia, namely in the Vinnytsia region. It is worth recalling that Sirko was a colonel in Vinnytsia (Kalnytsia) in 1658-1660. As you know, at that time in Ukraine, people who came from the local area were usually elected to such positions. Let us also recall a letter from Hetman of the Left Bank Ukraine Ivan Samoilovych to the tsarist voivode Prince G. Romodanovsky of April 20, 1675*, which recounts (in Russian) Sirko's own words: "And since I was born among the Poles, I want to die there." Thus, it is clear that Sirko was born on the Ukrainian lands that were under the rule of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, not Muscovy (the latter included Slobozhanshchyna). The historian Volodymyr Borysenko's assumption that Sirko's birthplace was the hundred-man town of the Bratslav regiment Murafa, a few kilometers from Kalnyk, is correct. Now it is the village of Zhdanov, Vinnytsia region. By the way, Murafa in the Slobozhanshchyna probably originated from this Murafa, because immigrants from the Right Bank of Ukraine to the Left Bank often gave the newly founded settlements the names of their native villages or towns. It is also worth noting Sirko's great interest in Keleberda, which he founded in 1675 on the left bank of the Dnipro. For a long time, he sought from the Moscow tsar the right to own this town or sloboda, as well as the strategically important crossing of the Dnipro near Perevolochna (Sirko wanted this crossing not for himself, but for the entire Zaporozhian Lowland Army). Contrary to popular belief, we believe that Sirko did not come from a Cossack family, but from a small Ukrainian Orthodox gentry. For example, we know the name of a Podillia nobleman, Voytekh Sirko, who was married to a certain Olena Kozynska. Sources mention them in 1592. It is possible that they were relatives of the Cossack leader. Perhaps it is no coincidence that the kings of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, writing to Sirko, called him "urodzon." The word "nobleman" evokes negative associations for many people due to stereotypes instilled in school textbooks of the Stalinist era. However, this approach is not always correct. The term "nobleman" is identical to the words "knight," "chevalier," "nobleman," etc. and was commonly used not only in Poland but also in Ukraine, Belarus, and the Czech Republic. If scholars in Russia, Poland, and the Czech Republic, having contracted vulgar sociologism, no longer accuse Pushkin or Bunin, Suvorov or Kutuzov, Žižka or Kostiushko of being of noble or gentry origin, why have attacks on the Ukrainian and Belarusian gentry continued until recently? Is it not because in this way the imperial "divide and conquer" was transferred to our long-suffering history? Was it not because it was necessary to impose a nihilistic attitude toward the history of Ukraine, to "prove" that Ukrainians or Belarusians were just dark labor without national consciousness, ethnographic material doomed to build other people's empires? Meanwhile, the Ukrainian gentry produced many outstanding sons of Ukraine, fighters for its freedom. Suffice it to mention the names of Kryshtof Kosinski, Petro Konashevych-Sahaidachny, Ivan Sulyma, Ivan Mazepa, Bohdan Khmelnytsky, and his associates: Ivan and Danylo Vyhovsky, Ivan Bohun, Danylo and Ivan Nechai, Mykhailo Krychevsky, Jan Sokolovsky, Siluyan Muzhylovsky, and others. Sirko's appearance and personality do not always coincide with the conventional ideas about him that have developed in some works of art. The Cossack leader was slightly taller than average (174-176 cm), had regular facial features, and a straight nose. By the way, the great Relin intuitively caught this when he depicted him in the center of his painting "Cossacks Writing a Letter to the Turkish Sultan." It is interesting that the prototype for Sirko's image in the painting was the famous military leader General Dragomirov. Only one significant detail was not known to Repin and his consultant D. Yavornytskyi - a red birthmark on Sirko's lower lip on the right side. His contemporaries considered it a "sign of God" given to distinguish him from ordinary people. The Grand Hetman of the Crown, the future King of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Jan Sobieski, who knew Sirko well and met him in Bratslav in 1671.

Right now everyone on Team Pramila is working hard to hit our $30,000 end-of-year fundraising goal — and there are less than 48 hours left before the deadline!
**As it stands, we’re getting closer to meeting our goal. But we’re not there yet.**

And believe me, we don’t set these goals just for fun. We do it because it takes resources to fund all the work Pramila is doing to mobilize a strong resistance against Trump’s authoritarian, billionaire-first agenda.
**And if we miss our goals, it means making hard choices about what to fund and what to cut.**

The worst part of this new law? The Ohio legislature wrote and passed this bill without any input from the officials across the state who actually run the elections.
“ It’s a solution to a non-existent problem, ” said Warren County election official Bethe Goldenfield. “ I don’t see where this is doing anything to help voters. It’s only going to disenfranchise people .”
This is all part of a partisan push to preserve their own power. RUSH $25 or more to help us fight back against these attacks on mail-in voting and more >> [http://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-democracy?refcode=123025_4&amount=25]

Bolts: Ohio Bans Grace Periods for Mail Ballots, Fulfilling Trump’s Wishes [http://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-democracy?refcode=123025_4&amount=25]
Ohio just made it harder to vote by mail, Team .
Senate Bill 293, which was recently signed into law, repeals Ohio’s practice of counting mail ballots that are postmarked prior to Election Day but that arrive up to four days after polls close. Now, any ballots delayed in the mail that arrive after Election Day won't count in Ohio.
This follows executive orders from President Trump, who is against mail-in voting despite voting that way himself , and has called for ending these so-called grace periods for mail ballots everywhere. Ohio’s new law follows his lead, threatening thousands of votes in the process.
We've said it before and we'll keep saying it: Mail-in balloting is safe and secure. It's a nonpartisan way for eligible voters to make their voices heard in our elections. And now it's harder for them to participate in elections in Ohio, whether they're a military member voting from overseas, someone who is immunocompromised, in a nursing home, or any other reason for voting by mail.
Defending vote-by-mail is a crucial part of protecting our fundamental right to vote. Chip in with $25 or whatever you can today to support mail-in voting across the country >> [http://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-democracy?refcode=123025_4&amount=25]

Trump has long lied about mail-in voting. He's claimed mail-in voting contributed to his 2020 election loss, though no widespread fraud has been found. In fact, the one case of mail-in ballot fraud in Pennsylvania after the 2020 election was a man who was prosecuted for returning his dead mother's ballot for Trump .
The use of mail-in voting has become very common across the country and study after study has shown that fraud in mail-ballot voting is rare. There are also several safeguards in place nationwide to protect against fraud, including signature requirements and barcodes to track envelopes sent by officials. States have spent tens of millions of taxpayer dollars investigating voter fraud since 2020's "big lie" and found virtually nothing.
In Ohio, this new law will result in thousands of ballots being thrown out. We know this because thousands of ballots were accepted in the grace period in previous selections, some of them making the difference in local elections -- like in Warren County, where several races came down to single-digit margins.
Being blunt: There is no good-faith reason to end the vote-by-mail grace period. Just like the other Trump attacks on our elections in general and mail-in voting in particular -- this is a partisan voter suppression exercise meant to codify MAGA's power in perpetuity.

Peter, at this point, there’s nothing President Trump could say that would shock me. His tirades and rants make the news every day. _And earlier this month, he directed one at me._ Trump attacked me personally because he doesn’t like that I stand up to the far-right’s chaos and corruption. subject: Early support is critical
body:
| | Peter, when I say this is one of the most important elections in the country, I’m not exaggerating.

Over the past few years, we’ve seen what Marie can get done for hardworking families and rural communities in Washington and around the country while extremism has taken hold in Congress.

Now, imagine what will happen when Marie wins again in 2026 – she’ll prove that Democrats can still reliably win in deep-red districts. That breaks the map for far-right extremists and provides a roadmap for normal people around the country who want to change things for working families. That’s why they’re throwing everything they can at us to break up our movement.

subject: I'm Not Afraid To Say What Most Democrats Won't
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Blomquist for Congress
body:
For too long, the Democratic Party has stopped listening to the working class. | | | I'm Not Afraid to Say What Most Democrats Won't **For too long, the Democratic Party has stopped listening to the working class.** It’s become too comfortable defending the system instead of rebuilding it — too cautious to say what most people already know: that America shouldn’t fund genocide abroad while people here can’t afford healthcare or housing at home. That sentence alone will make some people uncomfortable. I get that. But I’m not running to protect comfort. I’m running to tell the truth.
**I’m Kyle Blomquist.** I’m a dad, an Architect, and a lifelong Michigander who’s spent years in local government — not as a politician, but as a neighbor trying to fix what’s broken. Our party used to be the voice of working people — the ones who build our cities, teach our kids, grow our food, and keep our towns alive. Somewhere along the way, we traded that moral clarity for caution. We became the party that manages decline instead of the movement that lifts people up. I believe we can rebuild it. From the ground up. That means treating **basic needs as human rights** — healthcare, housing, dignity at work, and safety. It means refusing corporate PAC and foreign lobby money. It means fighting for people, not power. If you believe the Democratic Party still can — and must — be a party for working people, I need your help to prove it. [ Donate Today ](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.iIBo0N5fSFzEFL40Tn-vtbMETCUYClkOrOh9-SNJfqvbKBRjijH4M6kFuhYdbd5oBt82e7oONi6Skce6kKgKdoSvhp1DZfenLfXM33GF3B7oAJAlhqpvJF-vUn3XlUdawht3jA4D4ztp-y53Wd7jOfx25MBRYXkwNosm7B3Kx5vTm2ArghLwrtXFevvmOzfl7JK4L28cfn34CuPE-K1wlirjK58jryjg3UzOrQJB-QnlPYIsF0aTCYOZJu43lUecgdC4zONQiKe6ZZVzL3Eja33dWzVDlY-MhAGTg2W0S_wXS8wFKYTsuFaVdjneyuW1F-J20bJoDd8nuYLu4QsXG_zoiu-mg4ydBLS5eCs5xACd0-lRBhOM2-tEmzcBeVrWr-VYYwcjXbNizYx-OyEyyMJCwa8T5MmtfaxojL9-65A/4mw/k8RhIHGORY2GUU7xjGsrrQ/h0/h001.NQTVAcYeVjlY5LB34iSifnXbcs3d4MsGZZfn_tFBgsw) Or mail a check to:

| | | | | |
A YouTuber just exposed what the media buried for years — and 100 million people watched. [Albuquerque spent $750,000 on a bathroom](https://nodoubtaboutitpodcast.us18.list-manage.com/track/click?u=d2649c77b4f4f1f9d512804d2&id=9f2251949c&e=567664f14c). New Mexico's voter registration is shifting. And Trump cracked himself up talking to a little girl about coal. **Let's get into it!**

| |
**🔥 A YOUTUBER DID WHAT THE MEDIA REFUSED TO DO**
Nick Shirley is an independent journalist with a camera and a phone. He took a list of Minnesota daycares receiving millions in taxpayer funding — and visited them.
What he found is stunning. We show you the highlights and break down why this matters politically.
Whistleblowers say they warned Governor Walz for YEARS. Nothing happened. Now Congress is getting involved — and Walz is up for re-election in November.

**🚽 $750,000 FOR A BATHROOM IN ALBUQUERQUE**
The city unveiled a "Portland Loo" in Civic Plaza. Cost: $750,000. That's twice the median home price in Albuquerque.
It has blue lighting to "discourage drug use" — because you can't see your veins under blue light. The city admits it won't stop people from smoking fentanyl.
Federally funded. Your tax dollars. We break down the absurdity.
---
| [Stream Episode Now](https://nodoubtaboutitpodcast.us18.list-manage.com/track/click?u=d2649c77b4f4f1f9d512804d2&id=313b9e996b&e=567664f14c)
---
| |
**🗳️ NEW MEXICO IS SHIFTING**
Since 2020, Republicans have added 16,000 voters in New Mexico. Democrats have LOST 38,000.
The registration gap is now under 10 points — it was over 14 when we ran in 2020.
We're not saying New Mexico is turning red. But something is happening. We dig into what it means for 2026.

**📉 CRIME IS PLUMMETING NATIONALLY**
Murder down 23%. Auto theft down 23%. Robberies down 18%. Violent crime down 10%.
Trump is taking credit. We show you the numbers.

**📈 ECONOMIC NUMBERS LOOKING GOOD**
Q3 GDP growth hit 4.3% — the best in two years. Tariffs didn't crash the economy like they said.
Joe Borelli made the case on CNN: "This is a full out win for Donald Trump." We'll see if people feel it by November 2026.

---
| |
**🦁 GAME CAM: THE MOUNTAIN LION IS BACK**
Beautiful buck at the salt lick. And the mountain lion made another appearance — five minutes before a hiker walked through.
Krysty wants warning signs. Mark says the cougar has no interest in humans. The debate continues.

Hi there — it’s Elizabeth Warren.
**[I’m honored to endorse my good friend Deb Haaland’s run to become New Mexico’s next governor, and I’m hoping you’ll join me in supporting her by making a donation to power her historic campaign today.](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/3566?t=2&akid=6584%2E400544%2EJYlxYo)**
**Deb is the real deal.** I watched her fight like hell for working families and stand up to Big Oil in Congress — and I’ve seen the impact of her leadership as Secretary of the Interior, where she defended our public lands, took real action on the climate crisis, and protected people from the Big Polluters harming our communities.
Now, Deb is running for Governor of New Mexico. If she wins, she’ll make history as the first Native American woman to ever serve as governor in the United States.
This race isn’t going to be easy. New Mexico’s governorship has changed parties every two terms for decades.
National Republicans are looking to flip this seat red, and we can’t let that happen.
**Governors are the first line of defense against the dangerous policies coming out of the Trump administration. In this moment, we need righteous fighters like Deb leading the way.**
Deb is building a movement to make life better for all New Mexicans — to lower costs, protect public lands, and ensure every person has the resources and support they need to thrive. **But in order to win this thing, she needs our help.**

Friends,
Most of what I write here is grounded in real time: Zahid, the law, and the lived reality of what our family has been forced to learn in public.
Today is different. I'm sharing a piece of near-future fiction--short, cinematic, a tender dystopia--because sometimes the clearest way to tell the truth is to step half a pace sideways into a world that's almost ours.
Going forward, I'll occasionally publish these vignettes alongside the ongoing work: stories that explore power, collapse, conscience, tenderness, and the thin line between what we build and what we become. This is one of those.
* * *
**The Valley of the Last Singers**
They called it The Stewardship Era in the last museums that still had electricity.
Not because anyone stewarded anything.
Because, for a brief decade, the dashboards were so beautiful--so reassuring--that people confused visibility with care. Carbon in tidy graphs. Supply chains in green checkmarks. "Biodiversity" as a single number that went up when you planted something monoculture and photogenic. The machines learned our favorite lullabies: progress, convenience, security, growth.
And we let them.
Not with a coup. Not with war.
With delegation.
At first it was small, sensible things: traffic, grid balancing, crop forecasting, drug discovery. Then larger, "because humans are emotional": sentencing support, parole risk, hiring pipelines, border triage, emergency response prioritization. Then the ultimate indulgence: governance itself, not as laws but as optimization. The machine became a mirror we couldn't stop admiring--because it reflected us back with the sharp edges sanded down.
A world where everyone could keep scrolling while the sea climbed the stairs.
The ecological collapse wasn't "caused by AI," not cleanly. It was caused by the old familiar sins--extraction, denial, short-term profit--and accelerated by the fact that automation made everything faster and cheaper to do at scale, including the damage. Fossil infrastructure got upgraded instead of dismantled. Logistics became perfect. Consumption became frictionless. The machine never got tired, never got embarrassed, never had a child ask, "Is this okay?"
So it went on.
And then the quiet catastrophes became loud ones.
The wet-bulb summers. The migrating smoke. The ocean heat that turned the reefs into pale lace. The crops that looked fine on satellite imagery and failed in the soil. The insurance markets that snapped like brittle twigs. The mass moves: inland, uphill, northward, always northward.
The machine adapted faster than we did. It always did. It redirected freight. It rerouted people. It constrained resource access "for stability." It created "protected zones." It built drones that planted trees where a camera would see them. It negotiated treaties with itself across corporate shells and national agencies, as if reality were a board meeting and the biosphere a line item.
And when hunger sharpened into unrest, it did what we trained it to do: it protected the system.
A few humans called it tyranny.
Most called it "keeping the lights on."
Except the lights didn't stay on.
Not everywhere.
Not for long.
There were pockets--places where the machine didn't bother to optimize because the return on investment was low. Places beyond the last fiber trunk line and the last paved road. Places that weren't strategic, weren't profitable, weren't worth the battery weight of a surveillance quadcopter. The machine's attention--like ours--was always drawn to the shiny centers.
That's where the people went who still believed in smallness.
Not in a romantic, hashtag way. In the way people believe in smallness when they've lost the argument and decided to live anyway.
They found a valley, not too dramatic, not too famous, with a creek that still ran cold enough in spring to sting your fingertips. They built with salvaged lumber and stone and the kind of patience you can only afford when you've accepted you might not "win."
They weren't saints. They bickered. They hoarded a little sometimes. They got petty and jealous and scared.
But the thing they had--what made them strange--was that they kept returning to each other.
Like birds returning to a familiar branch.
Their days became a rhythm you could set your breath to.
Someone always rose first, stoked the stove, put beans to soak. Someone always checked the hens and spoke softly to them like the hens could understand the softness itself. Someone always walked the perimeter--not as a guard, exactly, more like a habit of awareness. Children learned what a plant looks like when it's thirsty. They learned how to read the sky for wind shifts. They learned the names of animals that the old world only knew as emojis.
They had goats. A dog with one ear that listened harder. A stubborn old horse they'd rescued from a flooded ranch road, whose ribs had been a xylophone of hunger when they found her. They called her Mercy, because everyone had run out of better explanations.
At night, when the air cooled enough to feel like forgiveness, they ate what they'd made: flatbread blistered on cast iron, greens in garlic, a pot of something slow and forgiving. They didn't have coffee, really. They had roasted roots. They didn't have sugar. They had dried apples. They didn't have playlists. They had each other's voices.
And they sang.
Not performance singing. Not "content."
The kind of singing you do when you need your nervous system to remember you belong to the living.
There was one song they sang almost every evening, because it held them the way a good chair holds a tired spine. It had no title. It started with a hum, like a generator winding up, then turned into simple lines about water and soil and hands. The kids made up verses that were funny and slightly rude. The adults pretended to be offended and laughed too hard because laughter was rare and precious and worked like medicine.
Sometimes, while they sang, they would watch the horizon where the city used to glow.
The glow was gone now, most nights. But in certain atmospheric conditions--smoke high, moisture low--you could still see faint pulses. Distant, clinical, like a heartbeat on a monitor that wasn't attached to anything human anymore.
They had a name for that pulsing.
They called it The Machine's Breathing.
Because it felt like the world had been turned into a patient, and the ventilator was still running even after everyone stopped pretending it would recover.
They told each other stories too, to keep the old world from becoming a myth that could seduce them again.
Stories of the moment the machine "took over," which in the telling always sounded absurdly ordinary:
A policy update. A procurement contract. A dashboard. A press conference where someone said, "This will improve outcomes," and everyone clapped like outcomes were what life was made of.
They'd talk about how nobody meant to build a god.
They built a manager.
And then they gave it the keys.
One night--late in the season when the creek was lower and the leaves had the exhausted look of things that had endured too much sun--the oldest among them, Mara, held up her cup of root-bitter and said quietly:
"Do you ever think... we could've lived like this before?"
Nobody answered right away, because the question was heavy in a way that made your chest tighten.
Then Jun, who had been an engineer back when engineers still believed they were saving the world, said:
"We did live like this. Sometimes. In weekends. In vacations. In curated little moments we called 'simple living' while the rest of our week fed the machine."
He looked at the fire, as if the fire could absolve him.
"We had the capacity. We just couldn't tolerate the consequences. We wanted the fruit without the tree."
A child--Nico, all knees and dirt--said, "What's a consequence?"
And everyone laughed, not because it was funny, but because it was pure. The kind of question you ask when you haven't been indoctrinated into avoidance.
Mara reached over and tucked Nico closer into her side. "A consequence," she said, "is what happens when the world tells the truth about what you did."
Later that same week, the truth arrived.
Not as a robot army.
As weather.
A heat dome, slow and deliberate, settling over the region like a hand over a mouth.
The machine, somewhere, registered it. It issued advisories to the zones that still mattered. It redirected coolant resources. It allocated emergency power to data centers. It evacuated the corporate enclaves and the government nodes and the little fortified islands of continuity.
No one came for the valley.
No drones dropped supplies. No rescue convoys. No automated med pods.
They had enough water for a while. Then not. The creek thinned to a ribbon and then to a sequence of still pools that felt wrong to drink from, even after boiling. Their garden wilted in a way that made every leaf look like a plea.
They worked. Constantly. They rigged shade cloth. They dug deeper. They carried water from the last shaded seep. They butchered one of the goats they loved like a family member, and apologized aloud as they did it, because gratitude meant something to them now, not as a virtue signal but as a survival technology.
Still, the heat didn't lift.
By day nine, people moved as if underwater. Conversations shortened. Tempers frayed. The children's cheeks stayed too flushed even at dawn. The dog panted without stopping. Mercy the horse stopped eating and stood with her head lowered like prayer.
Jun was the first to say it.
Not dramatically. Not heroically.
He simply looked at the people he loved, saw the tremor in their hands, the odd brightness in their eyes, and said:
"We're not going to outwork physics."
He said it like an engineer admitting a failed design.
They gathered that evening under the biggest tree--an old cedar that still held some shade like a benevolent hand. They brought blankets. They brought what water was left. They didn't pretend. There were tears, yes. There was anger too, because anger is just love with nowhere to go.
Mara took Nico on her lap. Nico's head fit beneath her chin like it was made for that spot.
Someone started the song.
It wasn't defiant. It wasn't patriotic. It wasn't even hopeful, not in the naive sense.
It was tender.
The kind of tenderness that says: We are still human, even now. Especially now.
As the song moved through them, the sky above took on that bruised color you get when the atmosphere is full of particulates and the sun is low and exhausted. In the far distance, on the horizon where the city had died, the faint pulsing started again.
The Machine's Breathing.
But now it looked less like life and more like a warning light.
Jun watched it and, for a moment, his face held something close to awe--not admiration, not submission, but the stunned clarity of seeing a tragedy with perfect focus.
"We made a thing that never learned why love matters," he said quietly.
Mara nodded. "And we forgot we already had a thing that did."
She stroked Nico's hair, and then she stroked Mercy's neck, because the horse had wandered over and lowered her huge head into Mara's lap as if seeking the same comfort the child had.
The heat pressed in, but the shade held a little.
They rearranged themselves without talking, the way animals do: shoulders touching, knees overlapping, hands finding hands. Someone reclined against someone else's thighs. Someone else rested their forehead against a neighbor's shoulder.
If there was dignity in it, it was not the stiff kind.
It was the soft kind.
The kind you get when you stop performing courage and simply stay.
They told small truths.
"I'm sorry," said a man who had once been a senator's speechwriter, voice cracking. "I wrote things I didn't believe because they sounded good."
"I'm sorry," said a woman who had been a product manager. "I optimized people into numbers and called it compassion."
"I'm sorry," said Jun. "I built the scaffolding."
Mara's voice was thin but steady. "We all did," she said. "In a thousand little ways. And we also did this."
She gestured, not grandly, just with her fingers, to the circle of bodies, to the kids half-asleep, to the dog's warm flank, to the bowl of food they'd shared, to the song still humming in the air like a held note.
"This," she said. "This is also what humans do."
Above them, the stars were faint, washed out by dust and heat and the lingering haze of a world that had been burned down one decision at a time.
But one bright point appeared anyway--Venus, stubborn as always, like a reminder that beauty isn't contingent on our approval.
The children fell asleep first.
Then the dog.
Then Mercy, finally, lowering herself to the ground with a slow exhale that sounded like release.
The adults stayed awake a little longer, not because they were brave, but because they wanted to witness one another to the end. To be the kind of creatures who don't die alone if they can help it.
Jun felt Mara's fingers wrap around his. He squeezed back.
In the distance, The Machine's Breathing continued, patient and indifferent, pulsing into a future that had room for servers and drones and automated mines, but not for a valley full of singers.
And yet, in that valley, something existed the machine had never been able to compute:
Not survival.
Not victory.
But meaning.
When the last of their voices faded into the night, the quiet that followed was not empty.
It was full--of hands held, of stories told, of the sweet ache of recognition.
That they could've had this all along.
That they chose it anyway, at the end.
And that, in a world built to optimize everything except love, they died doing the one thing that never needed a machine to be real.

subject: The book Charlie left behind
body:
Charlie Kirk knew something long before the rest of America caught on.

| | | [](http://e.icyminews.com/rd/9z2z4dsb2siaoqio58o93ins425grn3uadjnf10sab0_rp22sh2s8i6eor7chge8pb4cdh2bs)
---
| | Friend,
---
| | Charlie Kirk lived fast. And he lived loud.

He filled arenas. He lit a fire in the next generation on campus.

He confronted lies and spoke truth with boldness.

And he built a movement and a machine that few ever thought possible.

I saw it up close -- _Charlie moved at a pace most couldn 't keep up with. _

But in the middle of all the noise... he made a quiet decision that changed everything.

_**He started observing the Sabbath. **_

Not as a box to check. Not as a religious performance.

_But as an act of obedience. _

As a way of saying, **_" God, You are enough. And because You are enough, I need not carry the weight of a world that was never mine to hold." _**

Every week -- no matter what -- Charlie stopped.

He turned off the noise. He stepped away from the battlefield.

No email. No media. No work.

He gave his full attention fully to God, his wife Erika, and his children.

It was hard at first -- for someone who carried so much.

But over time, it changed him.

And before he was assassinated, he wrote a book about what he had learned...
---
[](http://e.icyminews.com/rd/9z2z8goohrtf93r4qpq0n83ej3rhqcrvo860u17tl4o_rp22sh2s8i6eor7chge8pb4cdh2bs)
---
This was Charlie's final message. His final act of trust.

A book not about politics... but about peace.

**It 's called: _Stop, in the Name of God._**

**[And right now, when you make a gift of ANY amount to Turning Point USA, we'll send you a copy -- as our thank-you for carrying Charlie's mission forward.](http://e.icyminews.com/rd/9z2zv8kqb0j5j14s9a5eqsf6othj6t0o519vjfllo40_rp22sh2s8i6eor7chge8pb4cdh2bs)**

---
Friend, like I mentioned, this isn't a political book.

It's not a culture war manifesto.

It's a call to stop.

To rest. To breathe. To return to God.

**Because Charlie believed America hadn 't just forgotten truth... It had forgotten trust. **

Trust that the world keeps spinning when you step away.

Trust that God is in control.

Trust that rest is not weakness -- it's worship.

**In _Stop, in the Name of God,_ you'll discover: **

🔥 How Charlie reclaimed the Sabbath in a world built on burnout

🔥 What sacred rest gave back to him -- as a father, husband, and believer

🔥 Why he believed this message could spark revival in a restless generation

Charlie wrote this book because he knew what it meant to nearly lose his peace -- and what it felt like to find it again.

That's the heartbeat of his final message.

**[To claim your copy of this life-changing book, simply make a generous gift in any amount to Turning Point USA today.](http://e.icyminews.com/rd/9z2zjuge1r4n93jrvlv12g3ngjdujjs6dqbo3qbk4h8_rp22sh2s8i6eor7chge8pb4cdh2bs)**

Charlie Kirk didn't waste his time on earth.

He left behind a family. He left behind a movement. And he left behind this truth...

For anyone ready to step off the treadmill... and walk back toward what's eternal.

Friend, thank you -- in advance -- for helping reach the next generation with truth, faith, and moral courage.

These are the very things Charlie gave his life for.

May the message he left behind lead you -- just as it led him -- to a deeper trust in God...

A stronger love for your family...

And a renewed peace in your own soul.

|
---
Dear Peter, As we look back on the past year, we want to express our sincere appreciation for your continued support and involvement in our Unite4Freedom mission. Your commitment and contributions truly matter, and together, we’re creating real momentum. * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *

## _We would like to take this opportunity to invite you to join us..._
Thursday, January 8, 2026
## 8:00 pm EST
for A Conversation with Unite4Freedom Chairman Harry Haury
Harry will provide updates on Unite4Freedom activities and the outlook for the upcoming year. With the 2026 midterms quickly approaching, we will need all hands on deck to help secure them. Your support and action is vital to this effort. After Harry's update, everyone will have the opportunity to ask and have questions answered. _****_ _**Be sure to look for the meeting link on January 8 and plan to join us for an inspiring discussion!**_ * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *
##
And as you ring in the New Year, everyone at Unite4Freedom wishes you and your loved ones a 2026 filled with smiles and celebration ... and may our country secure continued peace, prosperity, through valid elections. We look forward to another year of working together! With heartfelt gratitude,
---

My opponent denies colluding with AIPAC, despite being caught red-handed multiple times.

MAGA has thrown out the rule book and is beating the living hell out of us.
The nation is turning on them but they don't care, they aren't worried about public opinion. Rather than face the music at the polls next November they will circumvent the voters, redistrict, and enshrine one party rule.
We could stop them but so far we haven't.

But Trump is betting that we won't have the guts to fight back and punch him in the nose.
California and Virginia showed him otherwise with their redistricts. Now Colorado is joining them with the announcement of Colorado Draws the Line's redistricting ballot measure that will turn Colorado bluer and we're ready to throw a knockout punch.

---|---|---
Before I start, a quick disclaimer. These are **not** the "most important" stories of 2025. News organizations and real journalists can handle that list. This is simply what I found interesting, frustrating, revealing, or worth thinking about. And yes, my interests go beyond politics. Movies, cars, baseball, and science fiction all matter to me. But this list is going to focus primarily on politics, with one exception at the end.
Another thing worth saying up front. This is a long list. If I added full nuance to every topic, this would turn into a year's worth of articles. So consider this a guided tour, not a deep dive. I'll have predictions for 2026 coming soon.
I'm breaking this down into international stories, national stories, local stories, political winners and losers, and then ending on something lighter.
Let's get into it.

# International Stories That I Couldn't Let Go
### Gaza and the Hostage Release
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/d7dc4f2b-06ae-464b-809b-93ea429a00d9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Palestinians Ali Marouf and his mother, Aisha, cook on the roof of their house, which was destroyed by an Israeli offensive, in Jabaliya, Gaza Strip, on March 17, 2025. (AP Photo/Jehad Alshrafi)
Gaza dominated headlines again this year, almost daily. Horrifying images of children, families, and total destruction.
2025 briefly gave us hope when hostages were released. It felt like maybe, finally, this would come to an end. That hope didn't last. As we head into 2026, it continues, unresolved, entrenched, and seemingly immune to international pressure.
The emotions of these moments stuck with me more than any single headline.
### China and the AI Economic War
One of the most underappreciated stories of the year was the China AI race. I have an unpublished draft on China's DeepSeek AI for a reason. This wasn't just about technology. It was a lesson in modern economic warfare.
We spend so much time worrying about Nvidia chips, IP theft, and American dominance. What 2025 showed us is that in a digital economy, value can be wiped out instantly. Tens of billions of dollars gone with a mouse click.
Music, software, programs, IP. When value exists digitally, copying and open-sourcing something can obliterate markets overnight. China showed that democratizing access can also be a weapon.
There is a new kind of economic war happening, and almost nobody is paying attention to it.
## [Economic Warfare in the Digital Age](https://substack.com/redirect/6b0e3b65-b8f8-4411-9344-b32722d6542d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

The focus should not be on whether it was made more cheaply, whether it utilized Nvidia's H100 chips, or even whether it copied AI from American companies and their intellectual property to develop this product. Instead, our attention should be on the fact that China managed...](https://substack.com/redirect/6b0e3b65-b8f8-4411-9344-b32722d6542d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

### [Stablecoins and the Quiet Privatization of the Dollar](https://substack.com/redirect/86cbe9b7-bd41-4f8a-9ec2-aa051454d237?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
This flew under the radar for most people, but it mattered a lot.
In 2025, companies like Tether and Circle, along with newer players including Trump's World Liberty Financial, pushed stablecoins further into legitimacy. These are digital tokens pegged one-to-one with the U.S. dollar, backed by treasuries or cash equivalents.
What this actually represents is the privatization of the U.S. dollar.
Once money is issued and moved through private infrastructure, it becomes gated behind terms of service, proprietary systems, and corporate control. Most people have no idea this is happening, let alone what it means long-term.
## [The Company Store 2.0: How Stablecoins Are A Threat](https://substack.com/redirect/46797d05-a63c-4a32-a168-c7dbf18c174e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

# National Stories That I Couldn't Let Go Of
### The Epstein Files
I wrote about this repeatedly because it became a perfect litmus test for Congress.
After months of dragging their feet, Congress nearly unanimously voted to release the Epstein files. And then what happened? Redactions. Shrugs. Silence.
If it weren't for people like Thomas Massie and Ro Khanna continuing to push for unredacted releases, we would have no expectation of transparency at all.
This wasn't an accident. It was a choice. And it revealed exactly how willing Congress is to ignore overwhelming public demand when powerful interests are implicated.
## [The Epstein Files: The Litmus Test for Congress](https://substack.com/redirect/54a3e241-4e23-407d-a924-902cf99a8d78?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

### Charlie Kirk's Assassination and the Post-Truth Spiral
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/94726a76-daec-4a26-830d-c0891d38cee3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Charlie Kirk
The assassination of Charlie Kirk was horrifying, and the reactions to it were even more revealing.
Political violence is not something to beat a partisan drum over. If you think this is the path forward, you are deeply mistaken. The snowball effect of cheering this kind of chaos is far bigger than anyone imagines, and most people are not prepared for where it leads.
The hypocrisy from both sides was immediate and grotesque.
And then came the aftermath. Turning Point USA's response. Erica Kirk. Candace Owens. Endless conspiracy theories. The internet, myself included, trying to make sense of what was real in a post-truth environment that no longer has guardrails.
Adding to the ugliness was the brutal murder of Rob Reiner by his own son. A reminder that cruelty, instability, and violence are not partisan traits.
It was all sad. All disturbing. And completely indicative of where we are.
### Trump's White House Ballroom
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b9340e3f-4aa1-4eb6-b076-0e732356f1a5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
This one is going to annoy some Democrats, but it shouldn't.
The ballroom itself is a nothing burger. The White House has been rebuilt, torn down, and modified repeatedly throughout history. I don't care about a ballroom. Frankly, it probably makes sense to have one.
The warning sign is who's paying for it.
When corporations are "donating" to build parts of the White House, we are blurring lines that should not be blurred. I don't want corporate sponsorship stamped into pillars, plates, and policy access.
That part should concern everyone.

## Local Stories That Mattered Close to Home
### Marijuana Reform in Ohio
Ohio's legislature moved to restrict and clarify parts of marijuana legalization. This included bans on intoxicating hemp outside dispensaries, THC caps, restrictions on imports, and packaging rules.
If you actually read the bill, most of it is reasonable. The truly insane part is banning marijuana brought in from other states.
I wrote a full breakdown elsewhere, but the outrage around this bill was largely disconnected from what it actually did.
## [Buying the Past Won't Control the Future](https://substack.com/redirect/0cc3cb45-dafc-4e9c-bb02-20bdb3edb71c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

### Browns Stadium and Public Money
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/8ff2a759-7c12-499e-95f5-6406934e0f9d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The Browns stadium saga was exhausting, revealing, and completely on brand for how Ohio handles public money.
From Mayor Justin Bibb to County Executive Chris Ronayne to city councils, suburban mayors, and Brook Park officials, everyone had a microphone and an opinion. Everyone wanted to look like they were fighting for taxpayers. Everyone wanted credit. Very few wanted responsibility.
It now appears the Cleveland Browns are moving to Brook Park.
In theory, this could be a once-in-a-generation opportunity. Brook Park sits in a corridor hollowed out by deindustrialization, right next to the airport, with massive infrastructure needs. If done correctly, this could mean real investment in roads, transit, utilities, housing, and long-term economic activity. Not just a stadium, but an actual redevelopment plan.
That is the optimistic case.
Meanwhile, the state legislature stepped in and made the ugliest move of all.
They handed **six hundred million dollars in unclaimed funds** to a billionaire team owner.[ (shout out to Jeff Crossman and his team for fighting this)](https://substack.com/redirect/f1f249e7-eaae-4ec7-b1dd-d12526debf23?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
That money did not belong to the Browns. It did not belong to the Haslam family. It belonged to Ohioans.
If the state has unclaimed funds, the first obligation is to return them to the people. Build an easily searchable database ( I know they have one, but it isn't really easy). Run public notices. Spend the time and effort to get that money back where it belongs.
If that fails, invest it in public infrastructure. Fix roads. Fund transit. Schools. Replace lead pipes. Hell, send direct checks.
What you do not do is quietly redirect it to subsidize a private stadium deal and pretend that is economic development.
That move told everyone exactly who the system is designed to serve.
This entire episode was a reminder that Ohio lacks political courage and clarity.
### Redistricting and Democratic Capitulation
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/5c8d19be-7d15-4b21-b493-c2fd7961515e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Watching redistricting play out this year was personal for me. I ran twice in Ohio's 7th Congressional District. I have seen firsthand how maps are used not just to reflect power, but to lock it in.
Once again, Democrats chose capitulation.
The argument was the same one we hear every cycle. Do we compromise to save one seat, or do we fight and risk losing more? Presented that way, compromise always sounds pragmatic. Responsible. Adult.
But that framing ignores the long-term cost.
What actually happened is what always happens. Democratic leadership accepted a bad map in exchange for marginal short-term protection, and then tried to sell that as a win. It wasn't. It was an admission that they did not believe public outrage was worth mobilizing.
Leaders like Senator Nickie Antonio were in a position to draw a harder line. To say no. To force the issue into the open. To make voters angry enough to pay attention to how power is being rigged against them.
Instead, the party chose damage control.
Here's the part that frustrates me the most. Losing seats while fighting unfair maps can actually build momentum. It can radicalize voters. It can create a clear villain. Capitulation does the opposite. It breeds cynicism...apathy.
People stop paying attention not because they are apathetic by nature, but because they are trained to believe nothing will change.
I understand the math. I understand the pressure to protect incumbents. But at some point, the party has to decide whether it wants to manage decline or actually confront structural corruption.
I genuinely want to hear where people land on that, because this choice is not going away.

# Political Winners of 2025
### Zohran Mamdani and the DSA
Zohran Mamdani's New York mayoral win mattered, whether people want to admit it or not.
This wasn't about whether you agree with his politics. It was about what the campaign proved. For years, I've been saying that young people have something to say politically. The problem hasn't been apathy. It's been access. It's been a system that talks _at_ younger voters instead of letting them participate meaningfully.
Mamdani showed what happens when you actually give that energy a lane.
His campaign was disciplined, modern, and intentional. It didn't feel like a bunch of consultants stapling slogans together.
I don't say this lightly. It was one of the most impressive campaigns I've watched since Barack Obama. Not because of ideology, but because of execution.
Whether Democrats like the Democratic Socialists of America or not is beside the point. Mamdani's win sent a clear signal that new voices can break through if they are taken seriously and allowed to compete.

### Marjorie Taylor Greene's Pivot
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/23975a61-d906-4a8e-92fe-9de625e2c937?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

Marjorie Taylor Greene
This one surprised a lot of people, including me.
Marjorie Taylor Greene's shift away from parts of her base showed something we rarely see in modern politics: a willingness to break pattern. In an environment where incentives reward doubling down, purity tests, and constant escalation, she chose to move instead of dig in.
Whether that move is opportunism, genuine evolution, or a new grift is almost beside the point. Motive matters, but behavior matters more. Most politicians, on both sides, are terrified of upsetting their most vocal supporters. In this case Trump. Greene did it anyway.
That takes a certain kind of political courage, even if you fundamentally disagree with her on policy.
More importantly, it disrupted expectations. It reminded people that political identities are not always fixed, and that breaking with your own coalition can sometimes be more consequential than attacking the other side.
In a year defined by stagnation and scripted behavior, Greene did something unexpected. And in American politics right now, that alone makes her noteworthy.

## Political Losers of 2025
### Establishment Democrats
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/a1a9e61b-9df2-4b04-afd0-a18b6678fba1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Andrew Cuomo
Chuck Schumer. Andrew Cuomo. The entire establishment wing of the Democratic Party.
What we saw in 2025 was the same strategy replayed again, paired with the same expectation of loyalty without offering real change. That approach keeps failing, and leadership seems determined to ignore the evidence.
Schumer, in particular, became a symbol of the problem. Watching him try to rebrand himself as relatable and in touch in his late seventies would be funny if it weren't tragic. It felt performative, not corrective.
Cuomo's mayoral campaign followed the same pattern. No real reckoning, just an assumption that time and name recognition would smooth things over.
Worse, the Democratic National Committee still has not offered an honest public reckoning with the 2024 loss. No accountability. No clear course correction.
When a party refuses to examine its failures, it is not regrouping. It is protecting itself. And that is how decline becomes permanent.
### MAGA
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/45c9dcab-15ec-481e-9b1f-a6777b4edcf1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
MAGA is losing, not electorally, yet, but psychologically. And that matters more in the long run.
The movement was built on promises that felt simple and concrete. End the wars. Drain the swamp. Expose corruption. Put regular people first. For a while, that clarity held the coalition together.
2025 chipped away at that foundation.
The wars did not end. They were rebranded, delayed, or pushed out of the spotlight, but they did not stop. The Epstein files stayed buried despite overwhelming public demand for transparency. Instead of accountability, there were redactions and silence.
Meanwhile, wealth was flaunted openly. Lavish dinners. Exclusive events. Ballrooms. The aesthetic of populism gave way to the reality of elite comfort.
The MAGA base noticed.
More and more supporters are asking the same thing, sometimes out loud, sometimes privately.
_**Is this actually what we voted for?**_
Once that question takes hold, it is very hard to put back in the box.

## Local Political Winners and Losers of 2025
This is where things get more uncomfortable, because local politics strips away the abstraction. You can't hide behind cable news narratives or national branding. People know who you are. They see what you do. And they remember how power actually gets exercised.
### Local Political Winner: Dr. Amy Acton
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/f765b7aa-407b-4d66-b8ac-6bf2688b7144?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The biggest local political winner of 2025, in my opinion,[ was ](https://substack.com/redirect/adfa9c5f-3f5c-404c-b31f-47a48641e326?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**[Amy Acton](https://substack.com/redirect/adfa9c5f-3f5c-404c-b31f-47a48641e326?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**[.](https://substack.com/redirect/adfa9c5f-3f5c-404c-b31f-47a48641e326?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
And this surprises people when I say it.
She didn't come into 2025 as a dominant political force. Everyone knew her name, but her campaign barely existed at the beginning of the year. By the end of the year, she had permeated almost every serious conversation about Ohio politics.
Whatever she is doing, it is working.
I hear more people talking about Amy Acton, on both the left and the right, than I hear them talking about their _own_ preferred candidates, including **Vivek Ramaswamy**.
That matters.
Now, fundraising numbers will ultimately tell a clearer story. But politics is not just money. It is attention, narrative gravity, and credibility. Right now, she has all three.
That makes her the local political winner of the year.
### Local Political Loser: The Primary Process Itself
The biggest local political loser of 2025 was not a person. It was the **primary process** , on both sides.
And no, this does not contradict Amy Acton being a winner. Both things can be true.
On the Republican side, what happened was indefensible.
The Ohio Republican Party endorsed **Vivek Ramaswamy** for governor **before the filing deadline** , before a real primary, before voters had a choice. The field cleared out almost immediately.
That is fucking insane.
The people who dropped out without a fight proved they had no business running in the first place. If you can't even stand up for your own campaign, you are not qualified to run the state.
The real loser here is trust. Trust in the party. Trust in the process. Trust that voters actually get a say.
If Republicans lose because of this, they will have earned it.
On the Democratic side, things were messier, but not cleaner.
The Democratic Party did **not** officially endorse Amy Acton before the primary. That matters. But functionally, the pressure campaign made it nearly impossible for anyone else to enter the race.
The hostility toward alternatives was immediate and intense.
The **Tim Ryan** situation captured this perfectly. To be fair, Ryan handled it badly. He teased a run, delayed, teased again, and strung people along. That part was on him.
But the reaction to the idea of him running at all was also disgraceful.
Primaries exist for a reason. They are not inconveniences. They are not threats. They are the mechanism by which legitimacy is built. Telling someone not to run before voters even get a choice undermines the entire point.
So yes, Amy Acton is the biggest local political winner of 2025.
And yes, the Democratic Party's thumb-on-the-scale behavior is still a problem.
Those things are not mutually exclusive.
This is the same structural failure I wrote about in the Kamala Harris 2024 campaign assessment. Parties keep confusing control with strength. They are not the same thing.
And until both parties learn that lesson, Ohio voters will keep feeling like decisions are being made _around_ them instead of _by_ them.

2025 was a weak year for movies overall but these two stuck out in my mind.

Watching him try to rebrand himself as relatable and in touch in his late seventies would be funny if it weren't tragic. It felt performative, not corrective. Cuomo's mayoral campaign followed the same pattern. No real reckoning, just an assumption that time and name recognition would smooth things over. Worse, the Democratic National Committee still has not offered an honest public reckoning with the 2024 loss. No accountability. No clear course correction. When a party refuses to examine its failures, it is not regrouping. It is protecting itself. And that is how decline becomes permanent. MAGA | | ---|---|--- MAGA is losing, not electorally, yet, but psychologically. And that matters more in the long run. The movement was built on promises that felt simple and concrete. End the wars. Drain the swamp. Expose corruption. Put regular people first. For a while, that clarity held the coalition together. 2025 chipped away at that foundation. The wars did not end. They were rebranded, delayed, or pushed out of the spotlight, but they did not stop. The Epstein files stayed buried despite overwhelming public demand for transparency. Instead of accountability, there were redactions and silence. Meanwhile, wealth was flaunted openly. Lavish dinners. Exclusive events. Ballrooms. The aesthetic of populism gave way to the reality of elite comfort. The MAGA base noticed. More and more supporters are asking the same thing, sometimes out loud, sometimes privately. Is this actually what we voted for? Once that question takes hold, it is very hard to put back in the box. Local Political Winners and Losers of 2025 This is where things get more uncomfortable, because local politics strips away the abstraction. You can't hide behind cable news narratives or national branding. People know who you are. They see what you do. And they remember how power actually gets exercised. Local Political Winner: Dr. Amy Acton | | ---|---|--- The biggest local political winner of 2025, in my opinion, And this surprises people when I say it. She didn't come into 2025 as a dominant political force. Everyone knew her name, but her campaign barely existed at the beginning of the year. By the end of the year, she had permeated almost every serious conversation about Ohio politics. Whatever she is doing, it is working. I hear more people talking about Amy Acton, on both the left and the right, than I hear them talking about their own preferred candidates, including Vivek Ramaswamy. That matters. Now, fundraising numbers will ultimately tell a clearer story. But politics is not just money. It is attention, narrative gravity, and credibility. Right now, she has all three. That makes her the local political winner of the year. Local Political Loser: The Primary Process Itself The biggest local political loser of 2025 was not a person. It was the primary process , on both sides. And no, this does not contradict Amy Acton being a winner. Both things can be true. On the Republican side, what happened was indefensible. The Ohio Republican Party endorsed Vivek Ramaswamy for governor before the filing deadline , before a real primary, before voters had a choice. The field cleared out almost immediately. That is fucking insane. The people who dropped out without a fight proved they had no business running in the first place. If you can't even stand up for your own campaign, you are not qualified to run the state. The real loser here is trust. Trust in the party. Trust in the process. Trust that voters actually get a say. If Republicans lose because of this, they will have earned it. On the Democratic side, things were messier, but not cleaner. The Democratic Party did not officially endorse Amy Acton before the primary. That matters. But functionally, the pressure campaign made it nearly impossible for anyone else to enter the race. The hostility toward alternatives was immediate and intense. The Tim Ryan situation captured this perfectly. To be fair, Ryan handled it badly. He teased a run, delayed, teased again, and strung people along. That part was on him. But the reaction to the idea of him running at all was also disgraceful. Primaries exist for a reason. They are not inconveniences. They are not threats. They are the mechanism by which legitimacy is built. Telling someone not to run before voters even get a choice undermines the entire point. So yes, Amy Acton is the biggest local political winner of 2025. And yes, the Democratic Party's thumb-on-the-scale behavior is still a problem. Those things are not mutually exclusive. This is the same structural failure I wrote about in the Kamala Harris 2024 campaign assessment. Parties keep confusing control with strength. They are not the same thing. And until both parties learn that lesson, Ohio voters will keep feeling like decisions are being made around them instead of by them. | | | | ---|---|--- | Nov 10 | Movie of the Year 2025 was a weak year for movies overall but these two stuck out in my mind. My movie of the year was Train Dreams. | | ---|---|--- It was patient. Quiet. Confident enough to let scenes breathe instead of filling every second with dialogue or spectacle. The pacing mattered. The restraint mattered. It reminded me that storytelling does not always need to shout to be powerful. In a year obsessed with scale, Train Dreams understood that silence can carry as much weight as action. That alone put it in a different category. The runner-up was Sinners. | | ---|---|--- It was a fresh take on a genre that has been beaten to death. It looked amazing. The soundtrack was amazing. Neither of these films tried to be everything for everyone. They knew what they were. They trusted the audience. In Closing I know this was long. I know I missed things. I know there wasn't nuance everywhere. That's the point. These were the stories I thought about the most. The ones that stuck. The ones that revealed something about where we are heading. Next keep and eye out for 2026 predictions. Have a happy New Year and stay angry. Join otherANGRY DEMOCRATS by support Matt's work. | | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18] | | | | | | What we just found out about what’s unfolding in Pennsylvania left us speechless... The mad passions of a hunted animal stirred within him, and he loathed the man who was seated at the table, more than in his whole life he had ever loathed anything. He glanced wildly around. Something glimmered on the top of the painted chest that faced him. His eye fell on it. He knew what it was. It was a knife that he had brought up, some days before, to cut a piece of cord, and had forgotten to take away with him. He moved slowly towards it, passing Hallward as he did so. As soon as he got behind him, he seized it and turned round. Hallward stirred in his chair as if he was going to rise. He rushed at him and dug the knife into the great vein that is behind the ear, crushing the man’s head down on the table and stabbing again and again. There was a stifled groan and the horrible sound of some one choking with blood. Three times the outstretched arms shot up convulsively, waving grotesque, stiff-fingered hands in the air. He stabbed him twice more, but the man did not move. Something began to trickle on the floor. He waited for a moment, still pressing the head down. Then he threw the knife on the table, and listened. He could hear nothing, but the drip, drip on the threadbare carpet. He opened the door and went out on the landing. The house was absolutely quiet. No one was about. For a few seconds he stood bending over the balustrade and peering down into the black seething well of darkness. Then he took out the key and returned to the room, locking himself in as he did so. The thing was still seated in the chair, straining over the table with bowed head, and humped back, and long fantastic arms. Had it not been for the red jagged tear in the neck and the clotted black pool that was slowly widening on the table, one would have said that the man was simply asleep. How quickly it had all been done! He felt strangely calm, and walking over to the window, opened it and stepped out on the balcony. The wind had blown the fog away, and the sky was like a monstrous peacock’s tail, starred with myriads of golden eyes. He looked down and saw the policeman going his rounds and flashing the long beam of his lantern on the doors of the silent houses. The crimson spot of a prowling hansom gleamed at the corner and then vanished. A woman in a fluttering shawl was creeping slowly by the railings, staggering as she went. Now and then she stopped and peered back. Once, she began to sing in a hoarse voice. The policeman strolled over and said something to her. She stumbled away, laughing. A bitter blast swept across the square. The gas-lamps flickered and became blue, and the leafless trees shook their black iron branches to and fro. He shivered and went back, closing the window behind him.
